explanations.answer: A ringing gong or a clanging cymbal
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Paul says, "If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am only a ringing gong or a clanging cymbal." Picture the loudest, most impressive speaker ever, and without love it's just NOISE. Even angel-language turns into a smoke alarm when love is missing.

Nice picture, but it's not what Paul writes here. He says that without love, speaking in the tongues of men and of angels makes him only "a ringing gong or a clanging cymbal." Notice what those two have in common: they make a lot of sound. I think Paul wants us to hear how loud and empty that can be.

Good guess, but Paul doesn't say clouds anywhere in this verse. He says that if he speaks in the tongues of men and of angels but has not love, he is only "a ringing gong or a clanging cymbal." Those are instruments that make plenty of sound and no music. Talk about a band nobody asked to hear.

Yes, and Paul doesn't soften it. Prophecy, all mysteries, all knowledge and faith to move mountains, and then he says, "…but have not love, I am nothing." Look at that list, friend. It's the whole trophy shelf, and love is the one thing that makes it count.

Close in feel, but that's not Paul's word. He says that with prophecy, knowledge and mountain-moving faith but no love, "I am nothing." Honestly, someone who can move mountains sounds like the OPPOSITE of powerless. That's what makes his word hit so hard.

That's a sad one, but Paul doesn't say it. His word is stronger: with all that prophecy, knowledge and faith but no love, "I am nothing." He says nothing here about being remembered or forgotten. He's talking about what all those gifts add up to without love.

Right, and it stings a little. Paul writes, "If I give all I possess to the poor and exult in the surrender of my body, but have not love, I gain nothing." Giving everything away is a big deal, and he's not saying it's small. He's saying love is what the giving has to carry.

I get why this one feels backwards. Giving everything to the poor sounds like it has to count for something. But Paul says, "If I give all I possess to the poor and exult in the surrender of my body, but have not love, I gain nothing." So the statement is true: without love, he still gains nothing.

That's it. Paul says, "Love is patient, love is kind. It does not envy…" When somebody else gets the bigger blessing, love doesn't sit there counting. I'll be honest, I've seen a baker's cookie come out prettier than mine, and love says clap for them.

Fair thought, but that's not in Paul's list. He says, "Love is patient, love is kind. It does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud." Asking for the same as someone else is a lot closer to envy than to love. Love just doesn't go there.

That sounds patient, and love is patient. But the very next thing Paul says is, "It does not envy." So when someone else gets the bigger blessing, love doesn't stand there tapping its foot. It stays kind and doesn't envy.

Easy to flip that one around, friend. Paul actually says love "is not easily angered." It's in the same breath as "it is not rude, it is not self-seeking." So the statement is false. Love doesn't have a hair trigger.

Yes. Paul writes that love "is not rude, it is not self-seeking, it is not easily angered, it keeps no account of wrongs." Love isn't sitting there with its finger on the buzzer. Think of the calmest person you know in a traffic jam, and that's the direction Paul is pointing.

You got it, baker. Paul says love "keeps no account of wrongs." Somebody does you dirty, and love doesn't file it in a drawer for later. I know a thing or two about drawers, and that's one love never opens.

Good try, since love IS patient. But the verse reads, "it keeps no account of wrongs." Paul isn't talking about a clock here. He's talking about what love does when somebody does you dirty: it doesn't keep score.

I like that you're thinking about blessings, but that's not the word. Paul says love "keeps no account of wrongs." When somebody does you dirty, love doesn't hold it over their head. It lets the record go.
That's right. Paul says love "takes no pleasure in evil, but rejoices in the truth." Notice love has a happy side, too. It doesn't just turn away from evil, it celebrates what's true.
Not quite, friend. Paul says love "rejoices in the truth." Remember, he just said love "does not boast" and "is not self-seeking." A love that cheers for its own success wouldn't fit that list.

Ha, that's the opposite of where Paul goes. Right before this he says love "keeps no account of wrongs," so there's nothing to get even about. Then he says love "takes no pleasure in evil, but rejoices in the truth." Its joy is the truth, not payback.

Yes, sir. Paul says love "bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things." Hopes ALL things, not just the easy ones. That's four "all things" in a row, and he means every one.

I see why it might feel like a stretch, but it's right there. Paul says love "bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things." So the statement is true. Love hopes, and it hopes ALL things.

That's right. Paul says, "But where there are prophecies, they will cease; where there are tongues, they will be restrained; where there is knowledge, it will be dismissed." It's a long list, and love is the one on the other side of it. Right before, he says, "Love never fails."
Careful, friend, that line belongs to love. Paul says, "Love never fails." Then he turns to the gifts and says, "…where there are prophecies, they will cease." Love is the one that lasts.

I can see the logic, but Paul goes the other direction. He says, "…where there are prophecies, they will cease; where there are tongues, they will be restrained; where there is knowledge, it will be dismissed." The only thing he says never fails is love.

Yes! Paul says, "…but when the perfect comes, the partial passes away." Just before, he said we know in part and prophesy in part. So the partial is what gives way when the perfect arrives. Half a batch makes way for the whole thing.

Good guess, since prophecy is right there in the verses. But Paul says, "…but when the perfect comes, the partial passes away." He's setting the partial against the perfect, and the word isn't prophet. Keep it in the oven a little longer, friend.

Nice thinking, but harvest isn't in this passage. Paul says, "…but when the perfect comes, the partial passes away." He's talking about what we know and prophesy in part. When the perfect comes, that partial stuff is set aside.

It's the other way around, friend. Paul says, "When I was a child, I talked like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. When I became a man, I set aside childish ways." So he didn't hold on. He set them aside.
That's right. Paul says, "When I became a man, I set aside childish ways." He talked, thought and reasoned like a child, and then he grew up. Something partial gave way to something fuller.

Yes, that's it. Paul says, "Now we see but a dim reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face." A mirror gives you a blurry version, and face to face is the real thing. I think that's the part worth waiting for.

Close, but Paul skips the better mirror. He says, "Now we see but a dim reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face." Face to face means no mirror at all. That's a whole different level.
Nope, it goes the opposite direction. Paul says, "Now we see but a dim reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face." Face to face is as close as it gets. Distance isn't in the picture.
That's right. Paul says, "Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I am fully known." Right now it's a piece. Then it's the whole picture, and he'll know fully, just as he is fully known.

Easy to second-guess, but it's word for word in the verse. Paul says, "Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I am fully known." So the statement is true. He knows in part now, and then he'll know fully.

You got it, baker. Paul says, "And now these three remain: faith, hope, and love; but the greatest of these is love." Faith and hope stay too, so it's a strong lineup. Still, he names love as the greatest.

Faith is on the list and it remains, so I get why you picked it. Earlier Paul even mentioned faith that can move mountains. But he says, "And now these three remain: faith, hope, and love; but the greatest of these is love."

Hope is a good pick, and Paul does say it remains. He says, "And now these three remain: faith, hope, and love…" Then he finishes the thought: "…but the greatest of these is love." Hope stays, and love gets the top spot.
